 A Yankees reunion with Gary Sanchez needs a smaller role
 Alexander Wilson 
 Published : October 25, 2026 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Flipboard 
 Share via Email 
 Gary Sanchez hasn’t shut the door on the Yankees . Speaking with JoezMcfly before the World Series, he left a return open with a simple “you never know,” as the New York Post’s Mark Suleymanov reported Friday .
 I’d hear him out, provided everyone understands the job would be smaller this time. A useful second act would give New York another catching option and a right-handed bat, rather than ask Sanchez to become the everyday catcher fans remember from his first run.
 His comments aren’t evidence the Yankees have contacted him. He’s still with Milwaukee, and MLB’s upcoming free-agent list includes a mutual option. There is an availability decision to get through before anyone can start treating a reunion as an actual negotiation.
 The interesting part of Sanchez’s 2026 line isn’t the .209 average. He reached base at a .349 rate, hit 12 homers and drew 46 walks in 275 plate appearances. That’s a 16.7 percent walk rate, enough to make the offensive evaluation more useful than a glance at his average.
 Milwaukee regular-season archive, not a Yankees signing or a World Series interview photograph. Brewers catcher Gary Sánchez gestures as he circles the bases after hitting a two-run home run during the third inning against the Cardinals on Sunday, Sept. 27 at American Family Field. Credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect 
 The Yankees would be buying a different version of Sanchez
 Sanchez caught in 43 regular-season games for the Brewers, starting 38 of them. He also appeared at first base and DH. Whatever the Yankees might like about his bat, that workload doesn’t justify penciling him in to catch five days a week.
 The left-handed pitching split offers a more specific argument. Sanchez produced an .802 OPS in 123 plate appearances against lefties, compared with .747 against righties. That could fit a complementary assignment, though it isn’t enough of a sample to promise the same advantage next season.

 I’d want the Yankees to evaluate his receiving and throwing against the other available catchers before making a decision. A recognizable name shouldn’t win that comparison automatically, and New York shouldn’t need to reserve regular DH at-bats just to make a backup catcher signing work.
 The old expectations would have to stay behind
 The appeal is easy to understand. Sanchez can still draw walks and hit a mistake hard enough to change an inning. The harder part is agreeing on a role that matches the player he is now, with an honest allowance for the defense and workload the Yankees need from that roster spot.
 If his market requires starter money or an everyday assignment, I’d move on to another catcher. An affordable deal for a defined supporting job is worth investigating; another attempt to rebuild the lineup around the memory of his best Bronx seasons isn’t.
